title: Spin the Hour Hand 1, 2, 3… 20 Hours: Where Does It Stop? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: A big clock face (numbers 1–12, ≥ 48 px) with only an hour hand, pointing at 3. Line 1: tags '+1', '+2', '+3', '…', '+20' pop in a row beside the clock (the hand does NOT step: 3+1+2+3 would land on 9, the answer). Line 2: the hand spins as a fast blur and fades to a '?' without ever stopping on a number. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: Move a clock's hour hand one hour, then two, then three, all the way up to twenty.
Where does it stop? You won't need to spin it by hand!
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's go around the clock.

scenes.visual: Question text left, clock right with the hand at 3 (the hand stays still in this scene). Line 2: hand at 3 glows. Line 3: tags '+1', '+2', '+3' appear in a row. Line 4: tag '… +20'. Line 5: '?' on the clock. Line 6: choice chips 3, 6, 7, 9, 10.
lines: Here's the question.
The hour hand of a clock points to three.
Tom moves it forward one hour, then two hours, then three hours, and so on.
He finishes with a move of twenty hours.
To which number does the hour hand point at the end?
Here are the five choices.

scenes.visual: Line 1: tags '+1 +2 +3 … +20' in a row, '20 moves'. Lines 2–3: the hand does one full 12-hour turn back to 3, tag '12 hours = back where you started'. Line 4: tag 'goal: the final number'.
lines: There are twenty moves, and each one is one hour longer than the last.
Here's a key fact. Twelve hours is one full turn.
The hand lands right back where it started.
We want the number the hand points to at the very end.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; clock (hand at 3) and question visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Right panel. Line 1: tag 'add up all the moves'. Line 2: row '1 + 2 + 3 + … + 20'. Line 3: pairing arcs '1 + 20 = 21', '2 + 19 = 21', '3 + 18 = 21'… Line 4: '10 pairs × 21 = 210'.
lines: Welcome back! Let's add up all the moves first.
We need one plus two plus three, all the way to twenty.
Pair them up. One and twenty make twenty-one. Two and nineteen make twenty-one too.
Twenty numbers make ten pairs. Ten times twenty-one is two hundred ten hours.

scenes.visual: Line 1: row '210 ÷ 12 = 17 remainder 6' with '17 × 12 = 204', '210 − 204 = 6'. Line 2: the clock: 17 full turns shown as a fast spinning counter '×17' that ends back at 3. Line 3: the hand moves 6 more hours, one hour at a time from 3: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (label '+6'). Line 4: answer badge '3 + 6 = 9', chime at end, choice D highlighted.
lines: Twelve hours is a full turn. Two hundred ten divided by twelve is seventeen, remainder six.
Seventeen full turns bring the hand right back to three. They don't change anything!
Only the six leftover hours matter. Count six more from three.
The hand ends at nine. That's Choice D!

scenes.visual: The 20 moves as chips 1…20. Line 1: tag 'throw away 12s as you go'. Line 2: chips paired with arcs '1+11', '2+10', '3+9', '4+8', '5+7' each '= 12' and fading out. Line 3: chip 12 fades too. Line 4: chip '6' left glowing, hand from 3 → 9. Line 5: chips 13…20 each split '12 + 1' … '12 + 8', the 12s fade. Line 6: '1 + 2 + … + 8 = 36 = 3 × 12' fades. Line 7: hand stays at 9. Line 8: small text 'only leftovers matter'.
lines: Here's another way. Throw away full turns as you go.
One and eleven make twelve. So do two and ten, three and nine, four and eight, and five and seven.
And the move of twelve is a full turn by itself.
From the first twelve moves, only the six is left. So far, the hand goes from three to nine.
Each move from thirteen to twenty is a full turn, plus one to eight extra hours.
One through eight adds to thirty-six. That's three more full turns!
So the last eight moves change nothing. The hand stays at nine.
When would you pick this way? When you'd rather not add big numbers.

scenes.visual: Choice chips row; each turns red with a note. Line 1: chip B '6 = leftover, not the final number', small clock showing 6 hours counted from 12 vs from 3. Lines 2–3: chip A '3 = back to start?' with '210 ÷ 12 is not whole'. Line 4: chip C '7 needs leftover 4', chip E '10 needs leftover 7', vs '210 − 204 = 6'. Line 5: chip D '9' green.
lines: Now the traps. Choice B, six, is the leftover. It counts from twelve, but the hand started at three!
Choice A, three, says the hand ends where it started. That needs whole turns only.
But two hundred ten isn't a multiple of twelve.
Choices C and E, seven and ten, would need four or seven leftover hours. But the leftover is six.
Start at three, add six, and land on nine.

scenes.visual: Clock with the hand at 8. Card: 'moves 1, 2, 3, …, 16 hours. Where does it point?'.
lines: Ready for a challenge? This time the hand starts at eight.
It moves one hour, then two, then three, finishing with a move of sixteen hours.
Where does it point?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant clock visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: '1 + 16 = 17, 8 pairs'; '8 × 17 = 136'; '136 ÷ 12 = 11 remainder 4'; hand from 8 moves 4 hours: 9, 10, 11, 12; answer badge '12' chime at end of that line; tag '8 + 4 = 12 → the 12 itself'. Added line 'Eight plus four lands on the twelve itself.': '8 + 4 = 12' and tag on that line.
lines: Let's check. Pair them up: one and sixteen make seventeen, and there are eight pairs.
Eight times seventeen is one hundred thirty-six.
One hundred thirty-six divided by twelve is eleven, remainder four.
Count four hours from eight: nine, ten, eleven, twelve.
The hand points to twelve!
Eight plus four lands on the twelve itself.
If you got twelve, fantastic work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: clock with '12 = full turn', 'add all moves → keep the remainder → count from the start'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Add up all the moves. Full turns of twelve change nothing, so keep only the remainder.
Then count that many from where you started.
I'm Vantee. Keep spinning, and I'll see you next time!
